newsitem.title: UK: Oil share decline pauses but outlook unclear.
newsitem.headline: Oil share decline pauses but outlook unclear.

text.p: Oil company shares took a breather this week, but some analysts say they may still resume their fall which started last month after a strong 1996.
But any downward potential is limited as bid speculation will continue to underpin the smaller exportation and production (E&P) companies in particular.
"We believe the sector is fundamentally reasonable value in the longer term," said an analyst at a leading brokerage. "But there will be a better buying opportunity later in the year," he said.

He believes oil prices, which are relatively stable now after a two-month slide, will continue to fall again soon, dragging oil shares down. The price of North Sea Brent, the world benchmark crude oil, is hovering around $19.60 a barrel, well below a 1997 peak of $24.90.

Prices came under pressure from Iraq's return to world oil markets after the United Nations eased its ban late last year and mild winter weather in the northern hemisphere which dulled demand for heating fuel.
Nevertheless, some oil share watchers believe there is no clear correlation between oil prices and shares. They argue that news of takeovers and mergers is more likely to get the sector moving.
"It's a naive school which says that when oil prices go down, shares will follow," said Paul Spedding at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson.

The main reason why many shares in the oil exploration and production sector came off in February was a lack of bid news after Gulf Canada Resources Ltd gained control over Clyde Petroleum, Spedding said.
Nevertheless, many E&P stocks have lost their lustre in recent weeks after the sector pumped up some of the best performing stocks last year.
British-Borneo is one exception, gaining more than 60 percent so far this year. But the sector as a whole began to fall early in February and has lost an average 6.7 percent in value since then.

Some analysts say there is a downside for E&P shares of about eight percent if crude resumes its fall later this month, but others reckon a near-term price as low as $18 per barrel is already factored into the market.
